title: Why the Price Is What It Is: Reverse DCF, Valuation and Peers
web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
question: How much of HFC-32 and downstream growth is already in the ₹3,349.40 price?

epigraph.quote: FY28, on a conservative basis, given the full year production of HFC-32, the EBITDA margin will be around 24% to 26%.
epigraph.author: Afzal Malkani, Managing Director, Q2 FY27 call [6]

web_blocks.text: As of the verified November 13, 2026 BSE session, TANFAC closed at ₹3,349.40, with a snapshot market capitalization of ₹7,305.33 crore and TradingView trailing P/E of 99.32x. Screener’s rounded card showed ₹3,349 and P/E 104x; those feeds differ slightly, so the peer comparison below consistently uses the same TradingView/stock-snapshot extract rather than mixing providers. The company’s audited FY26 PAT was ₹70.14 crore and EPS ₹35.16; on that fiscal-year basis, the equity value is roughly 104x earnings, while the snapshot trailing multiple is lower because its TTM denominator includes later quarters. [1][12][34][35]

web_blocks.caption: Earnings bridge from filed FY26 actuals to management’s forward targets; the FY28 amounts below are calculated midpoint scenarios, not management-reported absolute revenue guidance. [1][4][6]
rows: November 3 call raised the earlier 30% guide; midpoint 37.5% applied to FY26 for an illustrative FY27 revenue of ₹977.73 crore. [6]
Midpoint 57.5% applied sequentially gives illustrative FY28 revenue ₹1,539.92 crore; not an absolute company forecast. [6]
At 25% midpoint, illustrative EBITDA is ₹384.98 crore. [6]

Illustrative PAT ₹259.48 crore, EPS ₹118.97 on 2.181 crore shares implied by same-session market cap/CMP; these are analyst assumptions, not guidance.
₹2,796, rounded to ₹2,800 per share; a material discount to the 44.27x median P/E of four screened peers reflects TANFAC’s smaller scale, cash conversion and project risks. [12][34]

web_blocks.text: This bridge is deliberately explicit so you can challenge every hinge. The company reports FY26 revenue ₹711.07 crore, then guided to 35–40% growth in FY27 and 55–60% in FY28 relative to FY27. Applying the midpoint rates yields about ₹1,540 crore in FY28, while the FY28 24–26% margin expectation yields about ₹385 crore EBITDA. We then assume ₹35 crore D&A, ₹8 crore finance cost, ₹4 crore other income and a 25% tax rate; estimated PAT is about ₹259 crore. The one-price share count is implied by market capitalization divided by close, not by a published forward consensus. A 23.5x multiple gives a base value just under ₹2,800. That multiple is intentionally far below Navin Fluorine’s and Gujarat Fluorochemicals’ current snapshot multiples because TANFAC has not yet reported a commercial HFC-32 run-rate or sustained post-capex free cash flow. [1][6][12][34]

web_blocks.caption: Same-session listed comparison set. These are not perfect peers: product mix, scale, liquidity and accounting differ; use valuation as context, not a mechanical target. [12][34][35]
web_blocks.takeaway: TANFAC’s 99.32x snapshot trailing P/E is about 2.24 times the four-peer median of 44.27x. The smaller Alufluoride multiple reflects a narrower, more commodity-linked business; Navin and Gujarat Fluorochemicals carry broader specialty/downstream platforms; SRF is diversified. TANFAC must earn its premium through actual downstream margins and cash, not project announcements alone. [12][29][34]

web_blocks.text: Peer selection is about mechanism, not resemblance by ticker. Alufluoride is the narrowest product comparator because it makes aluminium fluoride, but its small market capitalization and only 60 available daily bars leave a limited public technical history. Navin Fluorine is the specialty/CDMO scale reference: much larger, with a different portfolio and an established history of complex fluorination. Gujarat Fluorochemicals integrates refrigerants, fluoropolymers and battery materials, so it is a downstream breadth comparator. SRF is a diversified chemical and materials group; its lower multiple is not a direct read-through to TANFAC. The snapshot ratios also use each company’s current earnings cycle and should not be mistaken for normalized through-cycle values. [12][29][32][34]

web_blocks.the_number: At a 12% discount rate and 4% terminal growth, the current approximately ₹7,273 crore enterprise value requires about ₹904 crore of FY31 terminal FCFF under the stated five-year path.
web_blocks.how_calculated: We used analyst-specified FY27–FY31 FCFF of −₹100, ₹50, ₹250, ₹350 and ₹450 crore, discounted each year at 12%, then solved the Gordon terminal value backward from enterprise value (market capitalization less approximately ₹32 crore net cash). The deterministic calculation gives ₹606 crore present value for explicit cash flows, about ₹3,319 crore present value for a ₹450 crore terminal cash flow, and roughly ₹3,958 crore base equity value including net cash—about ₹1,815 per implied share.
web_blocks.the_inputs: Market capitalization ₹7,305.33 crore; September 2026 net cash approximately ₹32 crore; analyst FCFF path −100/50/250/350/450; WACC 12%; terminal growth 4%. Actual FY26 free cash flow was negative after capex, and FY28 includes further planned capex, so the path is an assumption, not a forecast. [1][4][6][12]
web_blocks.the_range: Required FY31 terminal FCFF is approximately ₹561 crore at 10% WACC / 4.5% growth, ₹904 crore at 12% / 4%, and ₹1,243 crore at 14% / 4%. The wide range exposes discount-rate and terminal-value sensitivity.
web_blocks.if_off: If management sustains margins, grows beyond the FY28 guide and converts more EBITDA to cash, terminal FCFF could exceed the base path and the DCF value rises sharply. If working capital and reinvestment remain heavy, a P/E-only valuation overstates owner cash. The reverse DCF is a hurdle test, not a target price.

web_blocks.title: Valuation conclusion
paragraphs: The market capitalization is not merely paying for today’s HF franchise. It prices a successful HFC-32 launch, 55–60% FY28 growth, 24–26% EBITDA margins and a later free-cash-flow stream. The price-blind business audit does not yet establish the cash economics needed to underwrite that full sequence. The base ₹2,800 value is below the ₹2,933–₹3,031 technical reference zone, so there is no support-level reward asymmetry to justify a wait-for-support buy. [1][6][7][12]

web_blocks.text: Reverse DCF and forward earnings tell different versions of the same caution. The forward earnings bridge can produce attractive FY28 EPS if management meets its targets, but even a 23.5x multiple yields only about ₹2,800. The DCF asks a harder question: recent free cash flow was negative after capex, and the market value requires a much larger terminal cash stream. In the base path, a ₹450 crore terminal FCFF supports materially less than the present enterprise value; even a low discount rate still requires about ₹561 crore. That difference can be bridged only by more scale, less working capital, higher margins, reduced growth capex or lower required return. None should be silently assumed. [1][4][6][12]

book_paragraphs: When you first see a P/E near one hundred, it is tempting to stop the analysis and call the shares expensive. That is a useful alarm, not a complete valuation. The company is investing in a product whose earnings may arrive after commissioning; trailing earnings are therefore backward-looking. But the opposite mistake is more common in a growth story: treating management’s best-case year as though it were already in the accounts. Our job is to price the interval between what is operating and what is promised. [1][6][12]

Let us build that interval carefully. FY26 revenue from operations was ₹711.07 crore. Management’s November call raised FY27 revenue-growth guidance to 35–40%, then described FY28 growth of 55–60% over FY27 and a 24–26% EBITDA margin. The midpoint arithmetic gives roughly ₹1,540 crore FY28 revenue and ₹385 crore EBITDA. Our bridge then subtracts assumed depreciation, finance cost, adds modest other income and applies a tax rate to reach estimated PAT around ₹259 crore. The calculation does not say management promised those rupees; it says what their percentages imply under our assumptions. [1][6]

At about 2.181 crore implied shares, that bridge yields EPS near ₹119. Apply 23.5 times—below the snapshot peer median because TANFAC has a smaller scale, lower public visibility and weaker demonstrated cash conversion—and you reach about ₹2,800. A more generous 30-times multiple gets nearer ₹3,600, but that already assumes the market will reward a new plant before its through-cycle cash record is visible. The current ₹3,349 price is therefore not absurd under a generous execution case, yet it offers no margin of safety under the more conservative base. [6][12][34]

Now try the cash question. I ask you to imagine that we are not buying a press release, but a stream of cash available after the plant is maintained, working capital is funded and future projects are paid for. TANFAC produced ₹43.4 crore operating cash in FY26 and spent ₹82.4 crore on property, plant and equipment, while management also discussed roughly ₹250 crore of future HF and solar-grade capex. We use an explicit five-year FCFF path and solve backward: at a 12% discount rate and 4% perpetual growth, the current enterprise value needs about ₹904 crore of terminal free cash flow by FY31. A ₹450 crore terminal stream supports only about ₹1,815 per implied share under the same DCF assumptions. [1][4][6]

That spread is not a scientific truth; it is the risk hidden in the terminal value. At a 10% discount rate and 4.5% growth, the required terminal cash flow falls to about ₹561 crore. At 14% and 4%, it rises above ₹1,240 crore. You can disagree with the discount rate, the capex path or the terminal growth. You cannot honestly pretend these choices are irrelevant. The market price asks you to believe that the product platform will grow past the FY28 plan and convert more of that growth to cash than the recent record has shown. [1][4][6]

The four peers are useful only after we define what they are not. Alufluoride is a small single-product reference with its own liquidity and customer risks. Navin Fluorine is much larger and has a mature specialty/CDMO platform. Gujarat Fluorochemicals has a broader fluoropolymer and refrigerant footprint. SRF is diversified beyond fluorochemicals. Their trailing P/Es span a wide range; the same-session median is about 44.27 times versus TANFAC’s 99.32. A median is not a fair-value law, but the premium demands a reason. The reason must be TANFAC-specific execution and cash, not the fact that fluorine has interesting applications. [12][29][34]

A useful way to test our conclusion is to change one assumption at a time. If you give TANFAC the same 44-times median multiple as the four screened peers, you are implicitly assuming that it already has comparable scale, business diversity, cash conversion and disclosure. It does not. If you instead award a premium for HFC-32, ask what evidence pays for it: the completion date, the first qualified batch, realized utilization, and the margin after imported feedstock and working capital. Each milestone could raise the probability of the bull case, but only a filed result should move the base estimate. The bear scenario is not a claim that management will fail; it is the cost of recognizing that a plant can be commissioned before its return on capital is known. [1][6][7][12]

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION — what must the price believe?
book_callouts.text: If you lower the terminal growth assumption or raise the cash-conversion haircut, does your base case still exceed the price? Write down the answer before treating HFC-32 capacity as an earnings asset.
